newsitem.title: UK: Israel sets sights on peace talks with Syria.
newsitem.headline: Israel sets sights on peace talks with Syria.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke on Tuesday about resuming stalled peace talks with Syria but reiterated the importance of Jerusalem as the nation's capital and the Golan Heights for its security.
In an interview with Britain's Channel 4 television news, he said Jerusalem had been the Israeli capital for 3,000 years.

"I haven't nailed the colours to Jerusalem. The Jewish people have nailed the colours to Jerusalem," he said. "There is no other attachment, anything like it...such an attachment of a people to a city and a place. It is unprecedented."

Asked if he would consider giving back some or all of the Golan Heights, which Israel seized from Syria in 1967, in exchange for peace, Netanyahu said he thought he should enter peace negotiations just as the president of Syria would.
"He demands all of the Golan Heights. So do I. We view the Golan as a critical area for Israeli security. Our view has not changed," he said.

Netanyahu, who has not made a secret of his eagerness to resume negotiations with Damascus, indicated that the United States might renew efforts for Israeli-Syrian talks following the inaguration of President Bill Clinton on Monday.
Netanyahu said the terroritorial issue would be on the table of any negotiations along with many other topics, including water, security and Lebanon.

"Hizbollah keeps attacking us from Lebanon and Syria is able to stop that and dismantle the military wing of Hizbollah and arrange for Lebanese Army deployment to the border. This is something I would like to see in the course of negotations with Syria."
Netanyahu's bid for new talks followed Israel's completion of its long-delayed Hebron deployment last week, considered by many as a major advancement in the Middle East peace process.

"We inherited an agreement and we honour agreements," he said. "In the case of the Golan Heights with Syria we inherited no agreement and therefore each side is free to bring to the negotiations whatever it chooses to bring," he added.
